title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: SolidAngleR package computes normalized solid angle measure polyhedral (simplicial) cones \(\mathbb{R}^n\) arbitrary dimension \(n \geq 2\). computational core implements five distinct algorithmic families, targeting specific class cone geometry: closed-form analytical formulas low dimensions, multivariable hypergeometric series cones positive definite associated matrices, tridiagonal specialization hypergeometric series cones whose Gram matrix banded structure, recursive decomposition method handles fully general case, multivariate normal integration via Quasi-Monte Carlo. vectorized C++ backend (via Rcpp RcppArmadillo) accelerates uniform cone sampling arbitrary dimensions. document describes mathematical foundations, numerical algorithms, software architecture, complete API surface package. Layered architecture SolidAngleR. cluster subsystem; arrows show flow user-facing inputs dispatcher computational backends C++ sampler.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Given \(n\) linearly independent vectors \(v_1, \ldots, v_n \\mathbb{R}^n\), simplicial cone \(C = \text{cone}(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = \{\sum_{=1}^n \lambda_i v_i : \lambda_i \geq 0\}\) traces region unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\). normalized solid angle measure \(\omega(C) \[0, 1]\) fraction \(S^{n-1}\) covered \(C\): \[ \omega(C) = \frac{\text{vol}_{n-1}(C \cap S^{n-1})}{\text{vol}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})} \] positive orthant \(C = \{x \\mathbb{R}^n : x_i \geq 0\}\), \(\omega(C) = 1/2^n\). methods package return normalized measure.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Central package associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) (Definition 1.1 Fitisone & Zhou [1]), constructed unit generators \(\hat{v}_i = v_i / \|v_i\|\): \[ M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{} = j \\ -|\hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_j| & \text{} \neq j \end{cases} \] positive definiteness \(M_n(C)\) determines whether hypergeometric series converges (Theorem 1.5 [1]). package computes \(M_n(C)\) via compute_associated_matrix() tests positive definiteness eigendecomposition tolerance \(\epsilon = 10^{-10}\).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Two dimensions. \(v_1, v_2 \\mathbb{R}^2\), solid angle planar angle rays, normalized \(2\pi\): \[ \omega = \frac{1}{2\pi} \arctan2\!\left(|\det[v_1, v_2]|,\; v_1 \cdot v_2\right) \] implementation uses atan2 correct quadrant handling returns 0 collinear opposite vectors. Colinear detection uses tolerance \(10^{-15}\) determinant magnitude. Implementation: R/formulas_2d.R exports solid_angle_2d(v1, v2). Three dimensions. \(v_1, v_2, v_3 \\mathbb{R}^3\), Euler-Lagrange formula [2] computes spherical excess: \[ E = 2\,\arctan2\!\left(\left|v_1 \cdot (v_2 \times v_3)\right|,\; 1 + v_1 \cdot v_2 + v_1 \cdot v_3 + v_2 \cdot v_3\right) \] \(\omega = E / (4\pi)\). numerator absolute value scalar triple product; denominator handles case \(1 + \sum \text{dot products} < 0\) atan2 branch cut. triple product smaller \(10^{-15}\), cone degenerate function returns 0. Implementation: R/formulas_3d.R exports solid_angle_3d(v1, v2, v3), solid_angle_3d_det(V) (matrix interface), spherical_triangle_area(v1, v2, v3) (returns \(E\) steradians rather normalized measure).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: \(n \geq 4\) \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, Ribando’s multivariable hypergeometric series [3] computes solid angle power series pairwise dot products \(\alpha_{ij} = \hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_j\): \[ \omega(C) = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{} \\mathbb{N}_0^N} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{}|}}{\mathbf{}!} \prod_{=1}^n \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1 + \deg_i(\mathbf{})}{2}\right) \right] \mathbf{\alpha}^{\mathbf{}} \] \(N = \binom{n}{2}\) number distinct pairs, \(\mathbf{} = (a_{12}, a_{13}, \ldots, a_{n-1,n})\) multi-index exponents, \(|\mathbf{}| = \sum a_{jk}\) total degree, \(\mathbf{}! = \prod a_{jk}!\), \(\deg_i(\mathbf{}) = \sum_{k \neq } a_{ik}\) degree vertex \(\) multigraph defined \(\mathbf{}\), \(\mathbf{\alpha}^{\mathbf{}} = \prod \alpha_{jk}^{a_{jk}}\). series converges absolutely \(M_n(C)\) positive definite. Convergence speed depends eigenvalue spread: nearly orthogonal cones (\(\alpha_{ij} \approx 0\)) converge terms, cones large dot products require many terms even \(M_n(C)\) positive definite. Algorithmic strategy. implementation enumerates multi-indices total degree \(d = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\), generating weak compositions \(d\) \(N\) parts via recursive backtracking. degree, degree contribution accumulated, convergence declared absolute change consecutive degrees falls tol. Specialized implementations \(n = 2\) (single-variable series \(\alpha_{12}\)) \(n = 3\) (three-variable series \(\alpha_{12}, \alpha_{13}, \alpha_{23}\)) avoid overhead general partition enumeration. Complexity. number weak compositions \(d\) \(N\) parts \(\binom{d + N - 1}{N - 1}\), grows combinatorially \(d\) \(N\). \(n \geq 5\) becomes expensive, though convergence typically occurs low \(d\) well-conditioned cones. Implementation: R/series_hypergeometric.R exports hypergeometric_series(V, max_terms, tol, check_pd) dispatcher, hypergeometric_series_nd(V, max_terms, tol) general \(n\)-dimensional engine, internal helpers hypergeometric_series_2d(), hypergeometric_series_3d(), compute_series_term_3d().

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Gram matrix \(V^T V\) tridiagonal (.e., \(\hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_j = 0\) \(|- j| > 1\)), hypergeometric series simplifies dramatically. summation reduces \(N = \binom{n}{2}\) variables \(n - 1\) consecutive dot products \(\beta_i = \hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_{+1}\): \[ \omega(C) = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{b} \\mathbb{N}_0^{n-1}} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{b}|}}{\mathbf{b}!}\, \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1+b_1}{2}\right) \prod_{=2}^{n-1} \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1+b_{-1}+b_i}{2}\right) \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1+b_{n-1}}{2}\right) \right] \mathbf{\beta}^{\mathbf{b}} \] Theorem 4.1 [1], tridiagonality \(V^T V\) implies \(M_n(C)\) automatically positive definite, series always converges. reduced dimensionality (\(n - 1\) instead \(\binom{n}{2}\)) yields substantial computational advantage, particularly high dimensions. Implementation: R/series_tridiagonal.R exports tridiagonal_series(V, max_terms, tol) internal compute_tridiagonal_term(b, beta). multi-index enumeration uses generate_partitions(n, k) R/utils.R.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, hypergeometric series converge. decomposition method, based Brion-Vergne theory [1], recursively partitions cone sub-cones, either positive definite associated matrix affine dimension less \(n\) (contributing zero solid angle). Algorithm. Given generators \(V = [v_1, \ldots, v_n]\): \(M_n(C)\) already positive definite, return \(V\) single terminal cone. Compute \(\delta_i = \text{sign}(\hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_n)\) \(= 1, \ldots, n-1\). \(\delta_i = 0\) (\(\hat{v}_n\) orthogonal generators), project onto \((n-1)\)-dimensional subspace orthogonal \(\hat{v}_n\) recurse. Otherwise, \(\) \(\delta_i \neq 0\), construct decomposed cone \(C_i\) generators: \[ u_{,k} = \begin{cases} v_k & \text{} \delta_k = 0 \text{ } k = \\ \epsilon_{ik}\left(v_k - \frac{v_k \cdot v_n}{v_i \cdot v_n} v_i\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] \(\epsilon_{ik}\) sign factor Equation 15 [1]. \(C_i\) carries sign \(s_i = \pm 1\) computed delta sequence. solid angle original cone \(\omega(C) = \sum_i s_i \cdot \omega(C_i)\). Recurse sub-cone whose associated matrix still positive definite. Corollary 3.4, decomposition produces \((n-1)!\) terminal cones. worst-case complexity therefore \(O(2^n)\), though well-conditioned cones typically decompose far fewer pieces. Implementation: R/decomposition.R exports decompose_cone(V, method), solid_angle_decomposition(V, max_terms, tol), internal helpers decompose_by_line(V), compute_epsilon(, k, delta).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Ribando’s approach [3] reformulates solid angle probability multivariate normal random variable falls positive orthant transformed coordinate system: \[ \omega(C) = \int_{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n} \phi_n(\mathbf{x};\, \mathbf{0},\, \Sigma)\, d\mathbf{x} \] \(\Sigma = (V^T V)^{-1}\) \(\phi_n\) \(n\)-dimensional Gaussian density. algorithm computes \(B = V^T V\), inverts obtain \(\Sigma\), evaluates integral via mvtnorm::pmvnorm(), uses Genz-Bretz Quasi-Monte Carlo algorithm [4] Halton sequences importance sampling. method works cone \(B\) positive definite, provides results exact numerical integration tolerance, avoids combinatorial explosion hypergeometric series. However, matrix inversion becomes ill-conditioned large \(n\) nearly dependent generators; function warns \(\kappa(B) > 10^{10}\) unreliable \(n > 20\). Complexity: \(O(n^3)\) matrix inversion plus \(O(M \times n^2)\) Quasi-Monte Carlo integration, \(M\) number adaptive quadrature points. Implementation: dispatcher branch compute_solid_angle(V, method = "mvn") (R/main_interface.R) computes \(B = V^\top V\), recovers \(\Sigma = B^{-1}\), forwards integral mvtnorm::pmvnorm(). function returns scalar normalized solid angle; per-dimension geometric mean recovered omega^(1 / ncol(V)) needed.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: package provides specialized formulas geometrically defined cones \(\mathbb{R}^3\) bypass general-purpose machinery. Right circular cones. Mazonka formula [5] (Equation 9) gives normalized solid angle cone apex half-angle \(\theta\): \[ \omega = \frac{2\pi(1 - \cos\theta)}{4\pi} = \frac{1 - \cos\theta}{2} \] Implementation: solid_angle_cone(theta) R/geometric_methods.R. Polyhedral cones (spherical polygons). Van Oosterom-Strackee formula [2] computes solid angle spherical triangle defined three unit vectors \(v_1, v_2, v_3\): \[ \tan\!\left(\frac{\Omega}{2}\right) = \frac{|v_1 \cdot (v_2 \times v_3)|}{1 + v_1 \cdot v_2 + v_1 \cdot v_3 + v_2 \cdot v_3} \] spherical polygons \(n > 3\) vertices, function decomposes triangular fans first vertex sums contributions. Implementation: solid_angle_polyhedral(vertices) R/geometric_methods.R. Cone segments. cone segment portion circular cone cut plane angle \(\gamma\) axis. Mazonka formula [5] (Equations 35, 39, 41) computes auxiliary angles: \[ \phi = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\cos\gamma}{\tan\theta}\right), \qquad \beta = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\theta}\right) \] solid angle \(\Omega = 2(\phi - \cos\theta \cdot \beta)\), normalized \(4\pi\). analytic expression yields negative invalid value, function falls back numerical integration spherical-cap intersection via stats::integrate() 2000 subdivisions. Implementation: solid_angle_cone_segment(theta, gamma) R/geometric_methods.R. Intersecting cones. two circular cones half-angles \(\theta_1\), \(\theta_2\) axis separation \(\alpha\), intersection solid angle computed numerical integration azimuthally admissible arc length: \[ \Omega = \int_0^{\theta_1} L(\theta)\,\sin\theta\,d\theta \] \(L(\theta) = 2\arccos C(\theta)\) \(C(\theta) = (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\alpha\cos\theta)/(\sin\alpha\sin\theta)\), clamped \([-1, 1]\). Special cases (overlap, containment, co-directed axes, opposite axes, hemisphere intersections) handled analytically falling back integration. Implementation: solid_angle_intersecting_cones(theta1, theta2, alpha, method, fallback, mc_samples, mc_seed) R/geometric_methods.R. L’Huilier’s theorem. spherical excess triangle arc-length sides \(, b, c\) : \[ E = 4\arctan\sqrt{\tan\!\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\tan\!\left(\frac{s-}{2}\right)\tan\!\left(\frac{s-b}{2}\right)\tan\!\left(\frac{s-c}{2}\right)} \] \(s = (+ b + c)/2\). provides numerically stable alternative Girard’s theorem \(E = \alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi\). Implementation: lhuilier_angle(, b, c) R/extreme_rays.R.

text: function \(\Theta: [0, \pi] \[0, 1]\) maps planar half-angle \(\theta\) fraction sphere enclosed corresponding cone: \[ \Theta(\theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}\,\!\left(\sin^2\theta;\, \frac{n-1}{2},\, \frac{1}{2}\right) & \theta \\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2}\,\!\left(\sin^2\theta;\, \frac{n-1}{2},\, \frac{1}{2}\right) & \theta \\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \end{cases} \] \((x; \alpha, \beta)\) regularized incomplete beta function, computed via pbeta(). inverse \(\Theta^{-1}\) uses qbeta(). piecewise definition avoids catastrophic cancellation near \(\theta = \pi/2\). Implementation: theta_to_omega(theta, n) omega_to_theta(omega, n) R/cone_sampling.R.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Given cone axis \(\hat{\mu} \S^{n-1}\) half-angle \(\theta_0\), uniformly distributed point spherical cap generated four steps: Step 1. Generate random planar angle. Sample \(\theta \[0, \theta_0]\) distribution \(F_\theta(\theta) = \Theta(\theta) / \Theta(\theta_0)\). Two methods available: Inverse transform sampling: generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \Theta(\theta_0))\) return \(\theta = \Theta^{-1}(U)\). Fast vulnerable floating-point underflow large \(n\) small \(\theta_0\). 1D rejection sampling: generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) \(\theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \theta_0)\); accept \(\log U < (n-2)[\log\sin\theta - \log\sin\min(\theta_0, \pi/2)]\). log transform prevents underflow. Expected number rejections \(O(n)\), maintaining overall \(O(n)\) complexity. Step 2. Generate perpendicular component. Sample \(\hat{x}_\perp\) uniformly \(S^{n-2}\) using Marsaglia method [7]: draw \(z_1, \ldots, z_{n-1} \sim N(0, 1)\) normalize. -loop rejects samples \(\|\mathbf{z}\| < 10^{-15}\). Step 3. Construct canonical vector. Form \(\hat{x} = (\sin\theta \cdot \hat{x}_\perp,\; \cos\theta)\) aligned \(n\)-th canonical basis vector \(\hat{e}_n\). Step 4. Rotate target orientation. Apply Givens rotation plane containing \(\hat{e}_n\) \(\hat{\mu}\): \[ \hat{y} = \hat{x} + P(G - I_2)P^T\hat{x} \] \(P = [\hat{e}_n,\; (\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n)/\|\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n\|]\) \(n \times 2\) orthonormal basis rotation plane \(G\) \(2 \times 2\) Givens matrix: \[ G = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_n & -\sqrt{1 - \mu_n^2} \\ \sqrt{1 - \mu_n^2} & \mu_n \end{bmatrix} \] rotation costs \(O(n)\) operations (two dot products two vector additions), unlike general \(n\)-dimensional rotation matrix cost \(O(n^2)\). Edge cases. \(\hat{\mu}\) nearly parallel \(\hat{e}_n\) (\(|1 - \mu_n^2| < 10^{-10}\)), second column \(P\) set zero, rotation reduces identity (parallel) reflection (antiparallel). implementation guards negative arguments sqrt via max(0, 1 - \mu_n^2). Hollow cones. algorithm extends annular regions \(\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2\) sampling \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(\Theta(\theta_1), \Theta(\theta_2))\) applying \(\theta = \Theta^{-1}(U)\). Implementation (R): R/cone_sampling.R exports generate_cone_sample(), generate_cone_samples(), generate_hollow_cone_sample(), generate_planar_angle_inverse(), generate_planar_angle_rejection(), rotate_from_canonical(), generate_point_on_sphere(), rejection_cost(), verify_cone_uniformity().

title: Hypergeometric and tridiagonal series and decomposition approaches
code: # Right angle (90 degrees) v1 <- c(1, 0) v2 <- c(0, 1) V_90 <- cbind(v1, v2) omega_90 <- compute_solid_angle(V_90)  # 45 degree cone v1 <- c(1, 0) v2 <- c(1, 1) / sqrt(2) V_45 <- cbind(v1, v2) omega_45 <- compute_solid_angle(V_45)  # Opposite rays (degenerate cone) v1 <- c(1, 0) v2 <- c(-1, 0) V_180 <- cbind(v1, v2) omega_180 <- compute_solid_angle(V_180) results_2d <- data.frame(   case = c("90° cone", "45° cone", "Opposite rays (degenerate)"),   computed = c(omega_90, omega_45, omega_180),   expected = c(0.25, 0.125, 0) ) results_2d$match <- ifelse(abs(results_2d$computed - results_2d$expected) < 1e-6, "✓", "✗") knitr::kable(   results_2d,   digits = c(NA, 6, 6, NA),   col.names = c("case", "computed", "expected", "match") )

code: # Orthogonal cone (octant) V_octant <- diag(3) omega_octant <- compute_solid_angle(V_octant)  # Narrow cone v1 <- c(1, 0, 0) v2 <- c(0.99, 0.1, 0) / sqrt(0.99^2 + 0.1^2) v3 <- c(0.99, 0, 0.1) / sqrt(0.99^2 + 0.1^2) V_narrow <- cbind(v1, v2, v3) omega_narrow <- compute_solid_angle(V_narrow)  # Compare formula vs. auto method omega_formula <- solid_angle_3d(v1, v2, v3) omega_auto <- compute_solid_angle(V_narrow, method = "auto") diff_methods <- abs(omega_formula - omega_auto) results_3d <- data.frame(   case = c("Octant (orthogonal)", "Narrow cone"),   computed = c(omega_octant, omega_narrow),   expected = c(0.125, NA_real_),   note = c(ifelse(abs(omega_octant - 0.125) < 1e-6, "✓ match", "✗ mismatch"),            ifelse(omega_narrow < 0.01, "✓ small", "✗ not small")) ) knitr::kable(   results_3d,   digits = c(NA, 6, 6, NA),   col.names = c("case", "computed", "expected", "note") ) method_table <- data.frame(   method = c("Formula", "Auto"),   omega = c(omega_formula, omega_auto) ) method_table$abs_diff <- c(NA_real_, diff_methods) method_table$agreement <- c(NA, ifelse(diff_methods < 1e-10, "✓", "✗")) knitr::kable(   method_table,   digits = c(NA, 8, 2, NA),   col.names = c("method", "omega", "abs. diff vs formula", "agreement") )

code: # Create tridiagonal cone with specified angles angles <- c(1.5, 1.5, 1.5)  # radians; moderate correlations for faster convergence V_trid <- create_tridiagonal_cone(angles)  # Verify structure VTV <- t(V_trid) %*% V_trid is_trid <- is_tridiagonal(VTV)  structure_table <- data.frame(   is_tridiagonal = ifelse(is_trid, "✓", "✗") ) knitr::kable(structure_table) knitr::kable(   round(VTV, 4),   col.names = paste0("v", 1:ncol(VTV)),   align = "c" ) # Compute using tridiagonal series result_trid <- tridiagonal_series(V_trid, max_terms = 500, tol = 1e-8)  # Compare with general hypergeometric series result_general <- hypergeometric_series(V_trid, max_terms = 500, tol = 1e-8) diff <- abs(result_trid$solid_angle - result_general$solid_angle)  trid_table <- data.frame(   method = c("Tridiagonal series", "General series"),   omega_normalized = c(result_trid$solid_angle, result_general$solid_angle),   converged = c(result_trid$converged, result_general$converged),   n_terms = c(result_trid$n_terms, result_general$n_terms),   abs_diff_vs_tridiag = c(NA_real_, diff) ) knitr::kable(   trid_table,   digits = c(NA, 6, NA, 0, 2),   col.names = c("method", "omega (normalized)", "converged",                 "terms used", "abs. diff vs tridiag") )

text: method based work Ribando (2006) [1], derived multivariable Taylor series expansion solid angle. simplicial cone \(C\) generated unit vectors \(v_1, \dots, v_n\), associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, solid angle given : \[ T_{\alpha} = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{}} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{}|}}{\mathbf{}!} \prod_{=1}^n \Gamma\left(\frac{1 + \text{deg}_i(\mathbf{})}{2}\right) \right] \alpha^{\mathbf{}} \] sum runs multi-indices \(\mathbf{} \\mathbb{N}_0^N\), \(N = \binom{n}{2}\). Implementing general \(n\) non-trivial requires iterating weak compositions integers \(N\) parts. package implements recursive generator solve combinatorial problem dynamically.

title: Exact analytical solid angles in higher dimensions
text: simplest approach solid angles orthogonal cone (orthant). dimension \(n\), normalized solid angle positive orthant exactly \(1/2^n\). can use validate high-dimensional series implementation.  error effectively zero (machine precision), confirming analytical correctness implementation \(n=4, 5, 6\). true power exact method becomes apparent compared Monte Carlo estimation. Monte Carlo unbiased noisy; error decreases slowly \(1/\sqrt{N}\). series method gives “ground truth” Monte Carlo converges. Let’s analyze 5-dimensional cone largely orthogonal satisfies convergence condition (Positive Definite associated matrix). Convergence prerequisite hypergeometric series.
code: library(SolidAngleR)  dims <- 4:20  results <- data.frame(   Dimension = integer(),   Exact_Theory = numeric(),   Computed_Series = numeric(),   Error = numeric() )  for (n in dims) {   # Orthogonal cone (Identity matrix)   V <- diag(n)      # Compute using the new generic series method   # For orthogonal cones, this is instantaneous as only the 1st term is non-zero   res <- hypergeometric_series_nd(V, tol = 1e-12)      theory <- 1 / 2^n      results <- rbind(results, data.frame(     Dimension = n,     Exact_Theory = theory,     Computed_Series = res$solid_angle,     Error = abs(res$solid_angle - theory)   )) }  # For orthants, the series collapses to the first term, so this table is a # strong sanity check on the n-dimensional implementation. # Print the numeric results table knitr::kable(   results,   digits = c(0, 10, 10, 2),   col.names = c("dimension", "exact theory", "computed series", "abs. error") ) # Set up the plot  library(ggplot2); library(patchwork) theme_v <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))  p_left <- ggplot(results, aes(Dimension)) +   geom_line(aes(y = Exact_Theory), colour = "#21908C", linewidth = 0.9) +   geom_point(aes(y = Computed_Series), colour = "#F89540",              shape = 19, size = 3) +   scale_y_log10() +   scale_x_continuous(breaks = dims) +   labs(title    = "Computed series vs. exact theory",        subtitle = "Simplicial orthogonal cones (orthants)",        x = "dimension n",        y = expression(paste("normalized solid angle ", omega)),        caption = "Source: hypergeometric_series() vs. analytic 1/2^n.") +   theme_v  p_right <- ggplot(results, aes(Dimension, Error)) +   geom_line(colour = "#E15759", linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(colour = "#E15759", shape = 17, size = 3) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = 2) +   scale_x_continuous(breaks = dims) +   labs(title    = "Numerical error trend",        subtitle = "Absolute error against the analytic value",        x = "dimension n",        y = "absolute error",        caption = "Floating-point precision check; values at machine epsilon.") +   theme_v  p_left + p_right set.seed(123) n <- 5  # Generate a 5D cone that is Positive Definite # We construct a matrix with small off-diagonal correlations. # For M to be PD, we need sum(|v_i . v_j|) < 1 for each row. # We use a very small off-diagonal value to ensure rapid series convergence # for this demonstration. off_diag <- 0.02 V_5d <- matrix(off_diag, n, n) diag(V_5d) <- 1 V_5d <- normalize_vectors(V_5d)  # Verify PD condition M <- compute_associated_matrix(V_5d) is_pd <- is_positive_definite(M) knitr::kable(   data.frame(quantity = "associated matrix positive definite",              value    = as.character(is_pd)),   caption = "Convergence prerequisite for the hypergeometric series." ) if (!is_pd) stop("Example cone must be PD for series method!")

title: Exact analytical solid angles in higher dimensions
text: Now run Monte Carlo simulations increasing sample sizes compare estimates exact value.  plot clearly shows Monte Carlo estimates oscillate around true value provided series method. high-precision requirements (e.g., p-values < 0.001), Monte Carlo method require millions samples, whereas series method gives answer instantly.
code: # Define cone test function for general simplicial cone cone_test_func <- function(x) {   # x is in cone if x = V %*% lambda with lambda >= 0   # equivalent to V^(-1) %*% x >= 0   coeffs <- try(solve(V_5d, x), silent = TRUE)   if (inherits(coeffs, "try-error")) return(FALSE)   all(coeffs >= 0) }  # Monte Carlo simulation sample_sizes <- c(1000, 10000, 100000, 500000) mc_estimates <- numeric(length(sample_sizes)) mc_errors <- numeric(length(sample_sizes))  # Use standard rejection sampling on the sphere (robust for general cones) # Note: For very narrow cones, this would be slow, but our cone is wide (~orthant) set.seed(42) for (i in seq_along(sample_sizes)) {   # solid_angle_monte_carlo returns result in steradians (unnormalized)   # We divide by surface area of unit sphere in 5D (8*pi^2/3) to normalize?   # WAIT: solid_angle_monte_carlo uses Marsaglia sampling on sphere and returns:   # Omega = Fraction * SurfaceArea   # Normalized Omega = Omega / SurfaceArea = Fraction      # But solid_angle_monte_carlo result$estimate is UNNORMALIZED (steradians for 3D).   # For generic n, we should implement a custom MC loop or interpret the result correctly.      # Let's implement a direct normalized MC loop here for clarity in n-dimensions   N <- sample_sizes[i]      # Generate N points on 5D sphere   pts <- matrix(rnorm(n * N), nrow = n)   pts <- apply(pts, 2, function(x) x / sqrt(sum(x^2)))      # Check containment   in_cone <- apply(pts, 2, cone_test_func)   count <- sum(in_cone)      p_hat <- count / N   se_hat <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / N)      mc_estimates[i] <- p_hat   mc_errors[i] <- se_hat }  library(ggplot2) df_mc <- data.frame(   log10N = log10(sample_sizes),   est    = mc_estimates,   lo     = mc_estimates - 2 * mc_errors,   hi     = mc_estimates + 2 * mc_errors )  ggplot(df_mc, aes(log10N, est)) +   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0,                 colour = "#3B528B") +   geom_line(colour = "#3B528B", linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(colour = "#3B528B", size = 2) +   geom_hline(yintercept = true_omega, colour = "#E15759",              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.7) +   labs(title    = "Convergence: exact series vs. Monte Carlo (5D)",        subtitle = "Monte Carlo estimate +/- 2 SE against the series value",        x = "log10(sample size)",        y = "normalized solid angle",        caption = "Source: hypergeometric_series() exact value (red dashed) vs. binomial MC.") +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))

text: series method offers analytical exactness, two key constraints must considered. First, positive definiteness condition requires series converges associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) positive definite; geometrically, means cone “narrow” (vectors highly correlated), condition violated, series diverge produce incorrect results. text: polyhedral cone defined vertices \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\) unit sphere, Van Oosterom & Strackee (1983) [2] formula provides: \[\Omega = \sum_{\text{faces}} \left( \sum_{\text{angles}} - (n-2)\pi \right)\] triangular face vertices \(\mathbf{}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}\): \[\Omega = \arctan\left(\frac{|\mathbf{} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|}{1 + \mathbf{} \cdot \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{}}\right)\]

title: Geometric methods for conical surfaces and intersecting spherical caps
text: acute cone valid intersection, define: \[ \phi = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\cos\gamma}{\tan\theta}\right), \qquad \beta = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\theta}\right). \] segment solid angle (steradians) : \[\Omega_{\text{segment}} = 2\left(\phi - \cos\theta \cdot \beta\right).\] report normalized value \(\omega = \Omega/(4\pi)\). Special cases: \(\gamma = 0\) returns full cone. \(\gamma > \pi/2 + \theta\), plane misses cone \(\Omega = 0\). \(\gamma > \pi/2\), symmetry gives equivalent angle \(\gamma_{\mathrm{eff}} = \pi - \gamma\). package implementation uses analytic expression valid falls back numerical integration near boundary cases.

text: cones can expressed geometrically polyhedral cones, can compare different computational methods:
code: # Create a cone that can be computed both ways theta <- pi/3 n_sides <- 8  # Approximate circular cone with octagonal cone  # Create octagonal cone vertices angles <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n_sides + 1)[-(n_sides + 1)] radius <- sin(theta) height <- cos(theta)  vertices_octagon <- rbind(   radius * cos(angles),   radius * sin(angles),   rep(height, n_sides) )  # Normalize to unit sphere vertices_octagon <- apply(vertices_octagon, 2, function(v) v / sqrt(sum(v^2)))  # Method 1: Geometric (circular cone) omega_geometric <- solid_angle_cone(theta)  # Method 2: Polyhedral (average over faces) omega_polyhedral_faces <- numeric(n_sides) for (i in 1:n_sides) {   j <- ifelse(i == n_sides, 1, i + 1)   face <- cbind(c(0, 0, 1), vertices_octagon[, i], vertices_octagon[, j])   omega_polyhedral_faces[i] <- solid_angle_polyhedral(face) } omega_polyhedral <- sum(omega_polyhedral_faces)  # Method 3: Algebraic (using 3D formula on apex vectors) # Create matrix from cone apex_vec <- c(0, 0, 1) V_cone <- cbind(apex_vec, vertices_octagon[, 1:2]) omega_algebraic <- solid_angle_3d(V_cone[, 1], V_cone[, 2], V_cone[, 3])  comparison_table <- data.frame(   method = c(     "Geometric (exact)",     sprintf("Polyhedral (%d-sided)", n_sides),     "Algebraic (3 vectors)"   ),   omega_normalized = c(omega_geometric, omega_polyhedral, omega_algebraic),   abs_error = c(0, abs(omega_polyhedral - omega_geometric),                 abs(omega_algebraic - omega_geometric)) ) knitr::kable(   comparison_table,   digits = c(NA, 6, 2),   col.names = c("method", "omega (normalized)", "abs. error") )

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Monte Carlo methods provide powerful alternative approach solid angle computation, particularly valuable analytical formulas unavailable complex geometric regions must analyzed. vignette presents rigorous exploration solid_angle_monte_carlo() function, examining theoretical foundations spherical Monte Carlo integration; convergence analysis varying sample sizes; error characterization uncertainty quantification; comparison analytical methods across dimensions; computational efficiency trade-offs; practical recommendations method selection. Monte Carlo approach estimates solid angles uniformly sampling points unit sphere computing fraction falling within region interest. conceptually simple, method exhibits rich statistical behavior worthy detailed investigation.

what: Monte Carlo integration on the sphere
title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: solid angle \(\Omega\) subtended region \(\mathcal{R}\) unit sphere \(S^2\) defined : \[\Omega = \int_{\mathcal{R}} dS\] \(dS\) differential surface area element. measurable region characteristic function \(\chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x})\) (equals 1 \(\mathbf{x} \\mathcal{R}\), 0 otherwise): \[\Omega = \int_{S^2} \chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dS\] Monte Carlo integration estimates integral : \[\hat{\Omega}_N = \frac{4\pi}{N} \sum_{=1}^{N} \chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x}_i)\] \(\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{=1}^N\) points sampled uniformly \(S^2\), \(4\pi\) total surface area unit sphere.

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Uniform distribution \(S^2\) requires equal probability density surface elements. Marsaglia method (1972) [1] achieves : Generate \(\mathbf{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_3)\) (3D standard Gaussian) Normalize: \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{z} / \|\mathbf{z}\|\) Theorem (Marsaglia, 1972 [1]): normalized Gaussian vector uniformly distributed unit sphere. Uniformity test sphere sampling.
code: #### Verify uniform sampling on sphere                                   #### set.seed(42) n_samples <- 10000  #### Generate samples                                                    #### points <- matrix(rnorm(3 * n_samples), ncol = 3) norms <- sqrt(rowSums(points^2)) points <- points / norms  #### Convert to spherical coordinates                                    #### theta <- acos(points[, 3])  # Polar angle phi <- atan2(points[, 2], points[, 1])  # Azimuthal angle  #### Test uniformity: cos(\u03B8) should be uniform on [-1, 1]              #### cos_theta <- points[, 3]  #### Kolmogorov-Smirnov test                                             #### ks_result <- ks.test(cos_theta, "punif", -1, 1)  uniformity_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Kolmogorov-Smirnov D",                "p-value",                "Conclusion"),   value = c(sprintf("%.6f", ks_result$statistic),             sprintf("%.6f", ks_result$p.value),             ifelse(ks_result$p.value > 0.05,                    "uniform distribution (p > 0.05)",                    "non-uniform (p < 0.05)")) ) knitr::kable(uniformity_table, caption = "Uniformity test for sphere sampling.") library(ggplot2) library(patchwork)  caption_text <- "Marginals of the uniform-on-sphere sampler. Generated by generate_point_on_sphere() in vignette d." theme_v <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))  p_cos <- ggplot(data.frame(cos_theta), aes(cos_theta)) +   geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,                  fill = "#3B528B", colour = "white") +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "#E15759",              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.7) +   labs(title    = expression(paste("Distribution of cos(", theta, ")")),        subtitle = "Empirical density vs. theoretical uniform marginal",        x = expression(cos(theta)), y = "density",        caption = caption_text) +   theme_v  p_phi <- ggplot(data.frame(phi), aes(phi)) +   geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,                  fill = "#21908C", colour = "white") +   geom_hline(yintercept = 1 / (2 * pi), colour = "#E15759",              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.7) +   labs(title    = expression(paste("Distribution of ", phi)),        subtitle = "Empirical density vs. theoretical uniform on [-pi, pi]",        x = expression(paste(phi, " (radians)")), y = "density",        caption = caption_text) +   theme_v  p_cos + p_phi

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Let \(p = \Omega / 4\pi\) true fraction sphere covered \(\mathcal{R}\). estimator \(\hat{p}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{=1}^N \chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x}_i)\) follows binomial distribution: \[N \hat{p}_N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, p)\] Expected value: \[\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Omega}_N] = 4\pi p = \Omega\] estimator unbiased. Variance: \[\text{Var}(\hat{\Omega}_N) = \frac{(4\pi)^2 p(1-p)}{N} = \frac{16\pi^2 p(1-p)}{N}\] Standard error: \[\text{SE}(\hat{\Omega}_N) = \frac{4\pi\sqrt{p(1-p)}}{\sqrt{N}} = O(N^{-1/2})\] Central Limit Theorem: large \(N\): \[\frac{\hat{\Omega}_N - \Omega}{\text{SE}(\hat{\Omega}_N)} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\] enables construction confidence intervals: \[\Omega \\left[\hat{\Omega}_N \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat{\Omega}_N)\right]\] \(z_{\alpha/2}\) standard normal quantile (e.g., \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\) 95% confidence).

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Monte Carlo error decreases \(O(N^{-1/2})\), independent dimension. contrasts deterministic quadrature rules, high-dimensional integration suffers “curse dimensionality.” achieve relative error \(\epsilon\), need: \[\frac{\text{SE}}{\Omega} \approx \epsilon \implies N \approx \frac{16\pi^2 p(1-p)}{(\epsilon \Omega)^2} = \frac{(1-p)}{p \epsilon^2}\] \(p = 1/8\) (orthant): \(N \approx 7/\epsilon^2\) 1% accuracy: \(N \approx 70{,}000\) 0.1% accuracy: \(N \approx 7{,}000{,}000\)
code: #### Test convergence rate for orthant (known \u03A9 = \u03C0/2)                #### set.seed(123)  orthant_test <- function(point) {   all(point > 0) }  sample_sizes <- 10^seq(2, 6, by = 0.5) n_replicates <- 50  omega_true <- pi / 2  # True value for orthant  results <- data.frame(   n_samples = integer(),   estimate = numeric(),   std_error = numeric(),   replicate = integer() )  for (n in sample_sizes) {   for (rep in 1:n_replicates) {     result <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(orthant_test, n_samples = round(n), seed = NULL)     results <- rbind(results, data.frame(       n_samples = n,       estimate = result$estimate,       std_error = result$std_error,       replicate = rep     ))   } }  #### Compute summary statistics                                          #### convergence_summary <- aggregate(   cbind(estimate, std_error) ~ n_samples,   data = results,   FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)) )  convergence_summary <- data.frame(   n_samples = convergence_summary$n_samples,   mean_estimate = convergence_summary$estimate[, "mean"],   sd_estimate = convergence_summary$estimate[, "sd"],   mean_std_error = convergence_summary$std_error[, "mean"] )  knitr::kable(   convergence_summary,   digits = c(0, 6, 6, 6),   col.names = c("n samples", "mean estimate", "sd estimate", "mean SE") ) library(ggplot2); library(patchwork) absolute_error <- abs(convergence_summary$mean_estimate - omega_true) relative_error <- absolute_error / omega_true ref_line <- relative_error[1] *   (convergence_summary$n_samples[1] / convergence_summary$n_samples)^0.5  df_left <- data.frame(   N         = rep(convergence_summary$n_samples, 3),   value     = c(relative_error,                 convergence_summary$mean_std_error / omega_true,                 ref_line),   series    = factor(rep(c("observed error", "theoretical SE",                             "N^(-1/2) reference"),                           each = length(convergence_summary$n_samples)),                      levels = c("observed error", "theoretical SE",                                  "N^(-1/2) reference")) )  theme_v <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))  p_left <- ggplot(df_left, aes(N, value, colour = series, linetype = series)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(data = subset(df_left, series == "observed error"), size = 2) +   scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +   scale_colour_manual(values = c("#3B528B", "#E15759", "#21908C")) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = c(1, 2, 3)) +   labs(title    = "Convergence rate: orthant solid angle",        subtitle = "Relative error vs. sample size on log-log axes",        x = "number of samples N",        y = "relative error",        caption = "Source: solid_angle_monte_carlo() with O(N^-0.5) reference.") +   theme_v + theme(legend.title = element_blank(),                   legend.position = "bottom")  df_right <- data.frame(   N    = convergence_summary$n_samples,   est  = convergence_summary$mean_estimate,   sd   = convergence_summary$sd_estimate )  p_right <- ggplot(df_right, aes(N, est)) +   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = est - sd, ymax = est + sd),                 width = 0, colour = "#3B528B") +   geom_line(colour = "#3B528B", linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(colour = "#3B528B", size = 2) +   geom_hline(yintercept = omega_true, colour = "#E15759",              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.7) +   scale_x_log10() +   labs(title    = "Estimate convergence",        subtitle = "Mean +/- SD across replicates against true orthant value",        x = "number of samples N",        y = "estimated solid angle (steradians)",        caption = "Dashed red line: orthant true value omega_true.") +   theme_v  p_left + p_right

text: Convergence rate analysis (log-log regression).
code: #### Verify O(N^{-1/2}) convergence empirically                          #### log_n <- log10(convergence_summary$n_samples) log_error <- log10(relative_error)  #### Fit linear model in log-log space                                   #### fit <- lm(log_error ~ log_n) slope <- coef(fit)[2] intercept <- coef(fit)[1]  convergence_rate_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Fitted slope",                "Expected slope (O(N^-1/2))",                "Difference",                "R-squared",                "Conclusion"),   value = c(sprintf("%.4f", slope),             "-0.5000",             sprintf("%.4f", slope - (-0.5)),             sprintf("%.6f", summary(fit)$r.squared),             ifelse(abs(slope - (-0.5)) < 0.1,                    "confirms O(N^-1/2) convergence",                    "deviates from expected rate")) ) knitr::kable(convergence_rate_table, caption = "Convergence rate analysis (log-log regression).")

what: Comparison of theoretical and empirical errors
title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Monte Carlo method provides theoretical error estimates via binomial statistics. verify empirical errors repeated trials. Error analysis across sample sizes (N_trials = 100 ).
code: #### Compare theoretical SE with empirical SD across sample sizes        #### n_test <- c(1000, 5000, 10000, 50000, 100000) n_trials <- 100  error_comparison <- data.frame(   n_samples = integer(),   theoretical_se = numeric(),   empirical_sd = numeric(),   mean_bias = numeric() )  for (n in n_test) {   estimates <- numeric(n_trials)   se_values <- numeric(n_trials)    for (i in 1:n_trials) {     result <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(orthant_test, n_samples = n, seed = NULL)     estimates[i] <- result$estimate     se_values[i] <- result$std_error   }    theoretical_se <- mean(se_values)   empirical_sd <- sd(estimates)   mean_bias <- mean(estimates) - omega_true    error_comparison <- rbind(error_comparison, data.frame(     n_samples = n,     theoretical_se = theoretical_se,     empirical_sd = empirical_sd,     ratio_sd_se = empirical_sd / theoretical_se,     mean_bias = mean_bias   )) }  knitr::kable(   error_comparison,   digits = c(0, 6, 6, 4, 6),   col.names = c("n samples", "theoretical SE (sr)", "empirical SD (sr)",                 "ratio SD/SE", "mean bias (sr)"),   caption = "Error analysis across sample sizes (N_trials = 100 each)." ) library(ggplot2) df_err <- data.frame(   N      = rep(error_comparison$n_samples, 2),   value  = c(error_comparison$theoretical_se, error_comparison$empirical_sd),   series = factor(rep(c("theoretical SE", "empirical SD"),                       each = nrow(error_comparison)),                   levels = c("theoretical SE", "empirical SD")) )  ggplot(df_err, aes(N, value, colour = series, shape = series)) +   geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(size = 2.4) +   scale_x_log10() +   scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E15759", "#3B528B")) +   labs(title    = "Theoretical vs. empirical error",        subtitle = "Binomial standard error vs. across-replicate sample SD",        x = "number of samples N",        y = "error estimate (steradians)",        caption = "Generated by solid_angle_monte_carlo() under repeat sampling.") +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0),         legend.title = element_blank(),         legend.position = "bottom")

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Confidence-interval coverage N = 50,000, 200 trials.
code: #### Test 95% confidence interval coverage                               #### n_samples_test <- 50000 n_trials_ci <- 200 alpha <- 0.05 z_critical <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)  # 1.96 for 95% CI  coverage_count <- 0  for (i in 1:n_trials_ci) {   result <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(orthant_test, n_samples = n_samples_test, seed = NULL)    ci_lower <- result$estimate - z_critical * result$std_error   ci_upper <- result$estimate + z_critical * result$std_error    if (omega_true >= ci_lower && omega_true <= ci_upper) {     coverage_count <- coverage_count + 1   } }  empirical_coverage <- coverage_count / n_trials_ci theoretical_coverage <- 1 - alpha  ci_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Sample size N",                "Nominal coverage (%)",                "Empirical coverage (%)",                "Coverage count (trials)",                "Binomial SE (%)",                "Conclusion"),   value = c(sprintf("%d", n_samples_test),             sprintf("%.1f", theoretical_coverage * 100),             sprintf("%.1f", empirical_coverage * 100),             sprintf("%d / %d", coverage_count, n_trials_ci),             sprintf("%.2f",                     100 * sqrt(theoretical_coverage * (1 - theoretical_coverage) /                                n_trials_ci)),             ifelse(abs(empirical_coverage - theoretical_coverage) <                      2 * sqrt(theoretical_coverage * (1 - theoretical_coverage) /                               n_trials_ci),                    "coverage matches expectation",                    "coverage deviates from expectation")) ) knitr::kable(ci_table, caption = "Confidence-interval coverage at N = 50,000, 200 trials.")

code: #### Compare MC with analytical for 2D angles                            #### angles_deg <- c(30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180) angles_rad <- angles_deg * pi / 180  n_mc <- 100000  comparison_2d <- data.frame(   angle_deg = angles_deg,   analytical = numeric(length(angles_deg)),   mc_normalized = numeric(length(angles_deg)),   abs_error = numeric(length(angles_deg)),   rel_error_percent = numeric(length(angles_deg)) )  for (i in seq_along(angles_rad)) {   angle <- angles_rad[i]   #### Analytical                                                         ####   omega_analytical <- angle / (2 * pi)    #### Monte Carlo (2D embedded in 3D)                                    ####   region_test <- function(point) {     #### Project to xy-plane                                              ####     x <- point[1]     y <- point[2]     z <- point[3]      #### Only consider points near z=0 plane                              ####     if (abs(z) > 0.1) return(FALSE)      #### Check if in angular wedge                                        ####     theta <- atan2(y, x)     if (theta < 0) theta <- theta + 2*pi     return(theta <= angle)   }    result_mc <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(region_test, n_samples = n_mc, seed = 42)    abs_error <- abs(result_mc$estimate / (4*pi) - omega_analytical)   rel_error <- abs_error / omega_analytical    comparison_2d$analytical[i] <- omega_analytical   comparison_2d$mc_normalized[i] <- result_mc$estimate / (4*pi)   comparison_2d$abs_error[i] <- abs_error   comparison_2d$rel_error_percent[i] <- rel_error * 100 }  knitr::kable(   comparison_2d,   digits = c(0, 6, 6, 6, 2),   col.names = c("angle (deg)", "analytical", "MC (normalized)",                 "abs. error", "rel. error (%)") )

code: #### Compare MC with analytical circular cone formula                    #### theta_values <- c(pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2, 2*pi/3) n_mc <- 100000  comparison_3d <- data.frame(   apex_angle_deg = theta_values * 180 / pi,   analytical_sr = numeric(length(theta_values)),   mc_sr = numeric(length(theta_values)),   se_sr = numeric(length(theta_values)),   abs_error = numeric(length(theta_values)),   rel_error_percent = numeric(length(theta_values)) )  for (i in seq_along(theta_values)) {   theta <- theta_values[i]   #### Analytical formula                                                 ####   omega_analytical <- solid_angle_cone(theta) * 4 * pi  # Convert to steradians    #### Monte Carlo                                                        ####   cone_test <- function(point) {     point[3] >= cos(theta)   }    result_mc <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(cone_test, n_samples = n_mc, seed = 42)    abs_error <- abs(result_mc$estimate - omega_analytical)   rel_error <- abs_error / omega_analytical    comparison_3d$analytical_sr[i] <- omega_analytical   comparison_3d$mc_sr[i] <- result_mc$estimate   comparison_3d$se_sr[i] <- result_mc$std_error   comparison_3d$abs_error[i] <- abs_error   comparison_3d$rel_error_percent[i] <- rel_error * 100 }  knitr::kable(   comparison_3d,   digits = c(1, 6, 6, 6, 6, 2),   col.names = c("apex angle (deg)", "analytical (sr)", "MC (sr)",                 "SE (sr)", "abs. error", "rel. error (%)") )

text: 3D simplicial cone comparison (N = 200,000).
code: #### Compare MC with Van Oosterom formula for triangular faces           #### test_cases <- list(   list(name = "Orthant",        V = diag(3),        expected = pi/2),   list(name = "Equilateral 60 deg",        V = cbind(c(1,0,0), c(0.5,sqrt(3)/2,0), c(0.5,sqrt(3)/6,sqrt(6)/3)),        expected = NA),   list(name = "Narrow cone",        V = cbind(c(1,0,0), c(0.99,0.1,0), c(0.99,0,0.1)),        expected = NA) )  n_mc <- 200000  simplicial_rows <- data.frame(   case = character(),   analytical_sr = numeric(),   normalized = numeric(),   mc_sr = numeric(),   se_sr = numeric(),   abs_error = numeric(),   rel_error_percent = numeric(),   within_3_sigma = character(),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  for (test in test_cases) {   V <- test$V   V <- normalize_vectors(V)    #### Analytical (Van Oosterom-Strackee)                                 ####   omega_analytical <- solid_angle_3d(V[,1], V[,2], V[,3]) * 4 * pi    #### Monte Carlo                                                        ####   simplicial_test <- function(point) {     #### Check if point is in positive cone                               ####     coeffs <- solve(V, point)     all(coeffs >= 0)   }    result_mc <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(simplicial_test, n_samples = n_mc, seed = 42)    abs_error <- abs(result_mc$estimate - omega_analytical)   rel_error <- abs_error / omega_analytical    simplicial_rows <- rbind(simplicial_rows, data.frame(     case = test$name,     analytical_sr = omega_analytical,     normalized = omega_analytical / (4*pi),     mc_sr = result_mc$estimate,     se_sr = result_mc$std_error,     abs_error = abs_error,     rel_error_percent = rel_error * 100,     within_3_sigma = ifelse(abs_error < 3 * result_mc$std_error, "yes", "no"),     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   )) }  knitr::kable(   simplicial_rows,   digits = c(NA, 6, 4, 6, 6, 6, 2, NA),   col.names = c("case", "analytical (sr)", "normalized", "MC (sr)",                 "SE (sr)", "abs. error", "rel. error (%)", "within 3 sigma"),   caption = "3D simplicial cone comparison (N = 200,000)." )

pi/2) / (pi/2)    mc_timing <- rbind(mc_timing, data.frame(     n_samples = n,     mean_time_ms = mean_time,     rel_error_percent = rel_error * 100   )) }  knitr::kable(   mc_timing,   digits = c(0, 2, 4),   col.names = c("n samples", "mean time (ms)", "rel. error (%)") ) #### Accuracy vs. computation time trade-off                             #### n_values <- 10^seq(2, 6, by = 0.2) times <- numeric(length(n_values)) errors <- numeric(length(n_values))  for (i in seq_along(n_values)) {   n <- round(n_values[i])    #### Time the computation                                               ####   timing <- system.time({     result <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(orthant_test_3d, n_samples = n, seed = 42)   })    times[i] <- timing["elapsed"]   errors[i] <- abs(result$estimate - pi/2) / (pi/2) }  library(ggplot2) df_eff <- data.frame(time_ms = times * 1000, rel_err_pct = errors * 100)  ggplot(df_eff, aes(time_ms, rel_err_pct)) +   geom_line(colour = "#3B528B", linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(colour = "#3B528B", size = 2.4) +   geom_hline(yintercept = c(1, 0.1, 0.01), colour = "#E15759",              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +   scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +   labs(title    = "Accuracy vs. computational cost trade-off",        subtitle = "Relative error of solid_angle_monte_carlo() against wall-clock time",        x = "computation time (ms)",        y = "relative error (%)",        caption = "Reference horizontal lines at 1%, 0.1%, 0.01% relative error.") +   theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))

code: #### Comprehensive validation study                                      #### validation_cases <- list(   list(     name = "Regular tetrahedron face",     V = cbind(c(1,0,0), c(0,1,0), c(0,0,1)),     method = "formula"   ),   list(     name = "60-60-60 deg spherical triangle",     V = cbind(       c(1, 0, 0),       c(0.5, sqrt(3)/2, 0),       c(0.5, sqrt(3)/6, sqrt(6)/3)     ),     method = "formula"   ),   list(     name = "Wide cone (120 deg opening)",     V = cbind(c(1,0,0), c(-0.5,sqrt(3)/2,0), c(-0.5,-sqrt(3)/2,0)),     method = "formula"   ) )  n_mc_validation <- 500000  validation_rows <- data.frame(   case = character(),   analytical_sr = numeric(),   mc_sr = numeric(),   se_sr = numeric(),   abs_error = numeric(),   rel_error_percent = numeric(),   z_score = numeric(),   assessment = character(),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  for (test_case in validation_cases) {   V <- test_case$V   V <- normalize_vectors(V)    #### Analytical                                                         ####   omega_analytical <- solid_angle_3d(V[,1], V[,2], V[,3]) * 4 * pi    #### Monte Carlo                                                        ####   cone_test_val <- function(point) {     coeffs <- tryCatch(       solve(V, point),       error = function(e) return(c(-1, -1, -1))     )     all(coeffs >= -1e-10)  # Small tolerance for numerical errors   }    result_mc <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(cone_test_val, n_samples = n_mc_validation, seed = 42)    #### Statistics                                                         ####   abs_error <- abs(result_mc$estimate - omega_analytical)   rel_error <- abs_error / omega_analytical   z_score <- abs_error / result_mc$std_error   assessment <- ifelse(z_score < 3, "excellent agreement",                        ifelse(z_score < 5, "acceptable", "poor agreement"))    validation_rows <- rbind(validation_rows, data.frame(     case = test_case$name,     analytical_sr = omega_analytical,     mc_sr = result_mc$estimate,     se_sr = result_mc$std_error,     abs_error = abs_error,     rel_error_percent = rel_error * 100,     z_score = z_score,     assessment = assessment,     stringsAsFactors = FALSE   )) }  knitr::kable(   validation_rows,   digits = c(NA, 8, 8, 8, 8, 4, 2, NA),   col.names = c("case", "analytical (sr)", "MC (sr)", "SE (sr)",                 "abs. error", "rel. error (%)", "z-score", "assessment"),   caption = "Comprehensive validation study (N = 500,000)." ) #### Final comparison plot: Analytical vs. MC                            #### theta_range <- seq(pi/12, 5*pi/6, length.out = 15) n_mc_final <- 200000  analytical_values <- numeric(length(theta_range)) mc_values <- numeric(length(theta_range)) mc_errors <- numeric(length(theta_range))  for (i in seq_along(theta_range)) {   theta <- theta_range[i]    #### Analytical                                                         ####   analytical_values[i] <- solid_angle_cone(theta) * 4 * pi    #### Monte Carlo                                                        ####   cone_test_final <- function(point) point[3] >= cos(theta)   result <- solid_angle_monte_carlo(cone_test_final, n_samples = n_mc_final, seed = 42)    mc_values[i] <- result$estimate   mc_errors[i] <- result$std_error }  library(ggplot2); library(patchwork) df_compare <- data.frame(   theta_deg = theta_range * 180 / pi,   analytical = analytical_values,   mc        = mc_values,   mc_lo     = mc_values - 2 * mc_errors,   mc_hi     = mc_values + 2 * mc_errors )  theme_v <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))  p_left <- ggplot(df_compare, aes(theta_deg)) +   geom_line(aes(y = analytical), colour = "#E15759", linewidth = 1) +   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mc_lo, ymax = mc_hi),                 width = 0, colour = "#3B528B") +   geom_point(aes(y = mc), colour = "#3B528B", size = 2) +   labs(title    = "Analytical vs. Monte Carlo",        subtitle = "Closed-form Mazonka cone vs. Monte Carlo +/- 2 SE",        x = "cone apex angle (degrees)",        y = "solid angle (steradians)",        caption = "Source: solid_angle_cone() vs. solid_angle_monte_carlo().") +   theme_v  rel_errors <- abs(mc_values - analytical_values) / analytical_values * 100 df_rel <- data.frame(theta_deg = df_compare$theta_deg, rel_err_pct = rel_errors)  p_right <- ggplot(df_rel, aes(theta_deg, rel_err_pct)) +   geom_line(colour = "#21908C", linewidth = 0.7) +   geom_point(colour = "#21908C", size = 2.4) +   geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.1, 0.5, 1.0), colour = "#E15759",              linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4) +   labs(title    = sprintf("Monte Carlo accuracy (N = %g)", n_mc_final),        subtitle = "Relative error against the analytical Mazonka value",        x = "cone apex angle (degrees)",        y = "relative error (%)",        caption = "Reference horizontal lines at 0.1%, 0.5%, 1.0%.") +   theme_v  p_left + p_right

text: solid angle \(\Omega\) quantifies three-dimensional angular extent subtended object point. Analogous planar angles, defined : \[\Omega = \frac{}{r^2}\] \(\) surface area projected onto sphere radius \(r\) centered observation point. unit solid angle steradian (sr), dimensionless quantity \(\text{sr} = \text{rad}^2\). Key properties: complete sphere subtends \(\Omega = 4\pi\) steradians; hemisphere subtends \(\Omega = 2\pi\) steradians; orthant (one-eighth sphere) subtends \(\Omega = \frac{\pi}{2}\) steradians. differential solid angle spherical coordinates \((\theta, \varphi)\) : \[d\Omega = \sin\theta \, d\theta \, d\varphi\] \(\theta \[0, \pi]\) polar angle \(\varphi \[0, 2\pi]\) azimuthal angle. arbitrary oriented surface \(S\), solid angle computed via surface integral: \[\Omega = \iint_S \frac{\hat{r} \cdot \hat{n}}{r^2} \, dS\] \(\hat{r}\) unit vector observation point surface element \(\hat{n}\) unit normal.

Let \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) denote interior angles \(, b, c\) opposite side lengths (measured arc lengths). spherical excess \(E\) defined : \[E = \alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi\]

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: Theorem (Girard, 1626 [9]): area \(\) spherical triangle sphere radius \(R\) equals \(R^2\) times spherical excess: \[\boxed{= R^2(\alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi) = R^2 E}\] unit sphere (\(R = 1\)), area equals excess directly. profound result connects intrinsic geometry (angles) extrinsic geometry (area). Proof sketch: Consider three lunes (double wedges) formed extending side complete great circle. lune angle \(\psi\) area \(4\psi R^2\). three lunes cover sphere cover triangle antipodal image three times : \[4\alpha R^2 + 4\beta R^2 + 4\gamma R^2 = 4\pi R^2 + 6A\] Simplifying yields Girard’s formula. Since solid angle unit sphere equals area, : \[\boxed{\Omega_{\text{triangle}} = \alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi}\] establishes fundamental connection solid angles spherical geometry.
code: #### Right spherical triangle (all angles = 90\u00B0)                     #### #### Each angle is \u03C0/2, so E = 3(\u03C0/2) - \u03C0 = \u03C0/2                       #### v1 <- c(1, 0, 0) v2 <- c(0, 1, 0) v3 <- c(0, 0, 1)  E_measured <- spherical_triangle_area(v1, v2, v3) E_girard <- 3 * (pi/2) - pi  # All angles are 90\u00B0 girard_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Measured area (sr)", "Girard's formula (sr)", "Normalized solid angle"),   value = c(E_measured, E_girard, E_measured / (4 * pi)) ) knitr::kable(   girard_table,   digits = c(NA, 6),   col.names = c("quantity", "value") )

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: Theorem (L’Huilier, 1789 [11]): spherical triangle sides \(, b, c\) semiperimeter \(s = \frac{+b+c}{2}\), spherical excess satisfies: \[\boxed{\tan\left(\frac{E}{4}\right) = \sqrt{\tan\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\tan\left(\frac{s-}{2}\right)\tan\left(\frac{s-b}{2}\right)\tan\left(\frac{s-c}{2}\right)}}\] spherical analogue Heron’s formula, enabling area computation side lengths alone without computing angles first. computational advantage makes L’Huilier’s theorem particularly valuable numerical applications.

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: polyhedral cone defined \(n\) unit vectors \(\{\mathbf{s}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_n\}\) (cyclic order), Mazonka derives remarkably efficient formula using complex arithmetic. Define vertex \(j\): \[a_j = \mathbf{s}_j \cdot \mathbf{s}_{j-1}, \quad b_j = \mathbf{s}_j \cdot \mathbf{s}_{j+1}\] \[c_j = \mathbf{s}_j \cdot (\mathbf{s}_{j-1} \times \mathbf{s}_{j+1})\] \[d_j = [\mathbf{s}_{j-1}, \mathbf{s}_j, \mathbf{s}_{j+1}] = \mathbf{s}_{j-1} \cdot (\mathbf{s}_j \times \mathbf{s}_{j+1})\] Main formula: \[\boxed{\Omega = 2\pi - \arg\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{n} (cb_j - a_j + d_j )\right\}}\] product complex numbers \(z_j = (cb_j - a_j) + d_j \). Key advantage: requires one arctangent operation (final argument), compared one per vertex traditional methods. Complexity O(n) constants dominated vector operations, transcendental functions.

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: \(n=3\) (triangular face), \(d_j\) equal: \(d_1 = d_2 = d_3 = d\). allows factorization: \[\Omega = 2\pi - \arg[(bc-+di)(ac-b+di)(ab-c+di)]\] Using \(d^2 = 1 + 2abc - ^2 - b^2 - c^2\) simplifying: \[\Omega = 2\pi - 2\arg[(1++b+c) + di]\] Therefore: \[\boxed{\tan\frac{\Omega}{2} = \frac{d}{1++b+c}}\] exactly recovers Van Oosterom-Strackee formula, demonstrating Mazonka’s approach unifies extends classical results.

Geometric construction: cone intersects unit sphere circle (spherical cap boundary); two circles intersect two points; plane intersection points cuts cap segments; total intersection solid angle equals sum two cap segments. Determining \(\gamma_1\): Using spherical trigonometry right triangles formed, robust form : \[\boxed{\gamma_1 = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\cos\alpha \cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2,\; \sin\alpha \cos\theta_1\right)}\] analogously \(\gamma_2\) (swap indices). \(\operatorname{atan2}\) form preserves sign quadrant information can lost plain \(\tan^{-1}\) expression. Total intersection: \[\boxed{\Omega_{\text{int}} = \Omega(\theta_1, \gamma_1) + \Omega(\theta_2, \gamma_2)}\] provides closed-form solution acute cones; practical implementations also handle special cases (hemispheres, containment, opposite axes) may fall back robust spherical-cap overlap integral analytic formula ill-conditioned.

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Generating uniform samples full sphere straightforward using Box-Muller transform (Marsaglia, 1972). However, sampling uniformly within spherical cap (base cone) presents fundamental challenges: Naive rejection sampling: cone half-angle \(\theta_0\) n dimensions, acceptance probability solid angle fraction \(\Omega(\theta_0)\). small \(\theta_0\) large n: \[\Omega(\theta_0) \approx \frac{\theta_0^{n-1}}{\sqrt{2\pi e}(n-1)}\] exponential decay makes rejection sampling prohibitively expensive high dimensions. example, 5-degree cone 100 dimensions requires approximately \(10^{150}\) samples per acceptance! O(n) algorithm Arun & Venkatapathi (2025) [1] solves problem generating samples directly within cone using elegant mathematical transformation involving incomplete beta function.
code: 1. Generate point uniformly on full sphere 2. Accept if point lies within cone 3. Otherwise reject and repeat

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Box & Muller (1958) [2] introduced fundamental method generating standard normal random variables, normalized produce uniform distributions spheres. Method: Box-Muller uniformity test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov). Theorem (Box-Muller): \(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) independent standard normal random variables, \[\hat{x} = \frac{(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_n)}{\sqrt{Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + \cdots + Z_n^2}}\] uniformly distributed unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\).
code: #### Generate uniform samples on 3D sphere                               #### set.seed(42) n_samples <- 5000  #### Box-Muller approach: normalize Gaussian vectors                     #### z <- matrix(rnorm(3 * n_samples), ncol = 3) norms <- sqrt(rowSums(z^2)) points_sphere <- z / norms  #### Verify uniformity                                                   #### cos_theta <- points_sphere[, 3] ks_test <- ks.test(cos_theta, "punif", -1, 1)  box_muller_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("KS statistic",                "p-value",                "Result"),   value = c(sprintf("%.6f", ks_test$statistic),             sprintf("%.4f", ks_test$p.value),             ifelse(ks_test$p.value > 0.05, "uniform", "non-uniform")) ) knitr::kable(box_muller_table, caption = "Box-Muller uniformity test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov).")

what: Why the O(n) algorithm is revolutionary
title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: 2025 method solves problem persisted 67 years: sample uniformly within cone without rejection. Previous approaches either used rejection sampling (exponentially inefficient narrow cones); required numerical integration lookup tables (accumulating errors); applied specific geometries (spherical triangles, 3D cones). incomplete beta function approach provides: Mathematical elegance: \[\Theta(\theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2\theta; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \[0, \frac{\pi}{2}] \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2(\pi - \theta); \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi] \end{cases}\] mapping \(\Theta: [0, \pi] \[0, 1]\) converts complex problem sampling \(f_\theta(\theta) \propto \sin^{n-2}(\theta)\) sampling uniform random variable applying inverse function \(\Theta^{-1}\). Computational efficiency: Numerical stability: algorithm uses log-space calculations incomplete beta function, avoiding underflow even extremely high dimensions (n = 200 tested), narrow cones (θ₀ = 0.001 radians), combined extremes cause \(\Omega_0 < 10^{-100}\). cases inverse transform becomes unstable (n > 80, narrow cones), fallback rejection method log-space ensures robustness.

Key mapping function: \(\Theta: [0, \pi] \[0, 1]\) \[\Theta(\theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2\theta; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \[0, \frac{\pi}{2}] \\[10pt] 1 - \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2\theta; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi] \end{cases}\] \((x; \alpha, \beta)\) regularized incomplete beta function: \[(x; \alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha, \beta)} \int_0^x t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1} dt\]

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: solid angle obtained integrating surface element: \[\Omega(\theta_0) = \frac{1}{s_n} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\pi \cdots \int_0^{\theta_0} \prod_{=1}^{n-2} \sin^\theta_i \, d\theta_{n-2} \cdots d\theta_1 \, d\phi\] Using Wallis integrals relationship beta function: \[\int_0^\theta \sin^m x \, dx = \frac{1}{2} B\left(\frac{m+1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right) \left(\sin^2\theta; \frac{m+1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\] telescoping products simplification, obtain stated formula \(\Theta(\theta)\). Inverse mapping: generation purposes, need \(\Theta^{-1}(\Omega)\): \[\Theta^{-1}(\Omega) = \begin{cases} \arcsin\sqrt{^{-1}(2\Omega; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})} & \Omega \[0, \frac{1}{2}] \\[10pt] \pi - \arcsin\sqrt{^{-1}(2(1-\Omega); \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})} & \Omega \(\frac{1}{2}, 1] \end{cases}\] \(^{-1}\) quantile function beta distribution (available qbeta() R).

text: uniform distribution spherical cap \(\mathcal{C}_{\theta_0}(\hat{\mu})\), planar angle \(\theta\) (measured \(\hat{\mu}\)) probability density function: \[f_\theta(\theta) = \frac{s_{n-1}}{s_n \Theta(\theta_0)} \sin^{n-2}(\theta) \quad \text{} \theta \[0, \theta_0]\] Intuition: density proportional surface area infinitesimal spherical shell angle \(\theta\), grows \(\sin^{n-2}(\theta)\). Cumulative distribution function: \[F_\theta(\theta) = \frac{\Theta(\theta)}{\Theta(\theta_0)}\]

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Given \(\theta_0\), generate \(\theta \[0, \theta_0]\) distribution \(f_\theta\). Method 1 (Inverse transform): 1. Generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \Omega_0)\) \(\Omega_0 = \Theta(\theta_0)\) 2. Return \(\theta = \Theta^{-1}(U)\) Method 2 (Rejection sampling log-space): 1. Generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) \(\theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \theta_0)\) 2. Accept \(\log U < (n-2)[\log(\sin\theta) - \log(\sin\theta_{\max})]\) 3. Otherwise reject repeat \(\theta_{\max} = \min(\theta_0, \pi/2)\). Advantage Method 2: Numerical stability large n small \(\theta_0\) (avoids underflow \(\Theta\)).

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Construct vector canonical orientation (aligned \(\hat{e}_n\)): \[\hat{x}_{\text{canonical}} = (\sin\theta \cdot \hat{v}, \cos\theta)\] rotate \(\hat{e}_n\) \(\hat{\mu}\) using O(n) Givens rotation 2D plane spanned \(\{\hat{e}_n, \hat{\mu}\}\).

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Input parameters O(n) cone sampler. Stage 1: random planar angle. Stage 2: perpendicular component. Stage 3: combine rotate. Computational complexity per sample.
code: #### Demonstrate each stage of the algorithm                             #### set.seed(42)  n <- 5 mu_hat <- c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0) / sqrt(3) theta0 <- pi/4  # 45 degrees  #### Stage 1: Generate planar angle                                      #### omega0 <- theta_to_omega(theta0, n) u_random <- runif(1, 0, omega0) theta_sample <- omega_to_theta(u_random, n)  #### Stage 2: Generate perpendicular component                           #### z_perp <- rnorm(n - 1) v_perp <- z_perp / sqrt(sum(z_perp^2))  #### Stage 3: Combine and rotate                                         #### x_canonical <- c(sin(theta_sample) * v_perp, cos(theta_sample)) x_rotated <- rotate_from_canonical(x_canonical, mu_hat)  input_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Dimension n",                "Cone axis mu_hat",                "Half-angle theta_0 (deg)",                "Solid angle fraction Omega_0"),   value = c(sprintf("%d", n),             paste(sprintf("%.3f", mu_hat), collapse = ", "),             sprintf("%.2f", theta0 * 180/pi),             sprintf("%.6f", theta_to_omega(theta0, n))) ) knitr::kable(input_table, caption = "Input parameters for the O(n) cone sampler.") stage1_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Random Omega ~ Uniform(0, Omega_0); U",                "Planar angle theta (rad)",                "Planar angle theta (deg)"),   value = c(sprintf("Omega_0 = %.6f; U = %.6f", omega0, u_random),             sprintf("%.4f", theta_sample),             sprintf("%.2f", theta_sample * 180/pi)) ) knitr::kable(stage1_table, caption = "Stage 1: random planar angle.") stage2_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Sphere S^(n-2) index",                "Random point v_hat",                "Norm ||v_hat||"),   value = c(sprintf("n-2 = %d", n - 2),             paste(sprintf("%.3f", v_perp), collapse = ", "),             sprintf("%.6f", sqrt(sum(v_perp^2)))) ) knitr::kable(stage2_table, caption = "Stage 2: perpendicular component.") stage3_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Canonical vector x_hat_can",                "Angle from e_n (rad)",                "Angle from e_n (deg)",                "Rotated vector x_hat",                "Norm ||x_hat||",                "Angle from mu_hat (rad)",                "Angle from mu_hat (deg)",                "Within cone?"),   value = c(paste(sprintf("%.3f", x_canonical), collapse = ", "),             sprintf("%.4f", acos(x_canonical[n])),             sprintf("%.2f", acos(x_canonical[n]) * 180/pi),             paste(sprintf("%.3f", x_rotated), collapse = ", "),             sprintf("%.6f", sqrt(sum(x_rotated^2))),             sprintf("%.4f", acos(sum(x_rotated * mu_hat))),             sprintf("%.2f", acos(sum(x_rotated * mu_hat)) * 180/pi),             ifelse(acos(sum(x_rotated * mu_hat)) <= theta0, "yes", "no")) ) knitr::kable(stage3_table, caption = "Stage 3: combine and rotate.") complexity_table <- data.frame(   stage = c("Stage 1 (angle generation)",             "Stage 2 (perpendicular; Box-Muller)",             "Stage 3 (rotation; Givens)",             "Total per sample"),   complexity = c("O(1) operations",                  "O(n) operations",                  "O(n) operations",                  "O(n) operations") ) knitr::kable(complexity_table, caption = "Computational complexity per sample.")

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: rotation \(\hat{e}_n\) \(\hat{\mu}\) performed using Givens rotation 2D plane containing vectors. Construction: Let \(\mu_n = \hat{\mu} \cdot \hat{e}_n\) n-th component \(\hat{\mu}\). Define orthonormal basis \(P\) rotation plane: \[P = \begin{bmatrix} | & | \\ \hat{e}_n & \frac{\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n}{\|\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n\|} \\ | & | \end{bmatrix} \\mathbb{R}^{n \times 2}\] 2D Givens rotation matrix : \[G = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_n & -\sqrt{1-\mu_n^2} \\ \sqrt{1-\mu_n^2} & \mu_n \end{bmatrix}\] rotated vector : \[\hat{y} = \hat{x} + P(G - I_2)P^T\hat{x}\] Complexity: requires O(n) operations (2 dot products, 1 matrix-vector product 2 columns). Givens rotation n = 3.
code: #### Demonstrate Givens rotation                                         #### n_rot <- 3 x_start <- c(0, 0, 1)  # Aligned with e_3 mu_target <- c(1, 1, 1) / sqrt(3)  # Target direction  x_rotated_demo <- rotate_from_canonical(x_start, mu_target)  givens_summary <- data.frame(   quantity = c("initial vector x_hat",                "target axis mu_hat",                "rotated vector y_hat",                "||y_hat||",                "y_hat . mu_hat",                "||y_hat|| ||mu_hat||"),   value    = c(paste(sprintf("%.3f", x_start),         collapse = ", "),                paste(sprintf("%.3f", mu_target),       collapse = ", "),                paste(sprintf("%.3f", x_rotated_demo),  collapse = ", "),                sprintf("%.6f", sqrt(sum(x_rotated_demo^2))),                sprintf("%.6f", sum(x_rotated_demo * mu_target)),                sprintf("%.6f", sqrt(sum(x_rotated_demo^2)) * sqrt(sum(mu_target^2)))) ) knitr::kable(givens_summary, caption = "Givens rotation in n = 3.") #### XY-projection of the rotation                                       #### theta_viz <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200) circle_df <- data.frame(x = cos(theta_viz), y = sin(theta_viz))  vec_df <- data.frame(   vector = factor(c("initial e_3", "target mu", "rotated y"),                   levels = c("initial e_3", "target mu", "rotated y")),   x      = c(x_start[1], mu_target[1], x_rotated_demo[1]),   y      = c(x_start[2], mu_target[2], x_rotated_demo[2]) )  label_df <- data.frame(   vector = vec_df$vector,   x      = vec_df$x * 1.10,   y      = vec_df$y * 1.10,   label  = c("hat(x)~(e[3])", "hat(mu)", "hat(y)") )  ggplot() +   geom_path(data = circle_df, aes(x, y), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +   geom_segment(data = vec_df,                aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y, colour = vector),                arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")),                linewidth = 1.0) +   geom_text(data = label_df,             aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, colour = vector),             parse = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE, size = 3.6) +   scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.85, name = NULL) +   coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.15, 1.15), ylim = c(-1.15, 1.15)) +   labs(x = "X", y = "Y",        title    = "Givens rotation (XY projection)",        subtitle = "rotation of e_3 onto the target axis mu_hat = (1, 1, 1)/sqrt(3)",        caption  = "Source: rotate_from_canonical(); the unit circle is the equator of S^2.") +   theme_minimal() +   theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8, hjust = 0))

angles_rejection <- acos(samples_rejection[n_comp, ])  #### Statistical comparison                                              #### ks_comparison <- ks.test(angles_inverse, angles_rejection)
